summary:
Antioquia department stands under Colombia's national legal framework, which is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, and national identification documents carry trans and non-binary markers from November 2025. A comprehensive trans law was still under legislative consideration in 2025.

The gap between that framework and enforcement is severe. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders in Colombia between January and May 2025 alone. The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025, praising the government's legal reforms and commitment to equality while warning that institutional progress and daily lived experience are disconnected, and that widespread discrimination and violence against LGBT people must be addressed urgently as killings rise.

Antioquia contains the city at the centre of the country's most alarming recent record on anti-trans violence. On 4 April 2025 in Bello, a city in Antioquia near Medellín, the 32-year-old trans woman Sara Millerey González Borja was beaten and thrown into a waterway in broad daylight while onlookers filmed her. The video went viral from 5 April, showing her with fractured limbs flailing in a creek unable to swim. She died of cardiac arrest the following afternoon. President Gustavo Petro ordered an urgent investigation, solidarity events were held in several cities, and protests followed. She was the third LGBTQ person killed in Bello during 2025; the first two victims were gay men. Her mother Sandra Borja stated that they killed her for being who she was.

Care access in the same episode is documented: a clinic reportedly did not treat her as an emergency because she had not been shot. One report counted 13 trans people killed in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025 alone, alongside 41 transgender women killed in 2023 and eight more between February and April 2024.

Where armed groups operate, the risk is structured rather than incidental. In the department of Caquetá, where ex-rebel structures persist despite the 2016 peace agreement, armed groups distributed flyers on streets and on WhatsApp announcing a 'social cleansing' plan naming 'faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes' as legitimate military targets, and threatened a further wave; trans women there fled after death threats. In the department of Guajira, armed groups posted flyers from March 2024 carrying a kill list of named individuals under the wording 'All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans'. In Caquetá, trans women reported few options beyond sex work; Tatiana Céspedes, a trans salon owner, was forced to relocate twice after death threats from armed men, and a friend of the trans woman Yesenia Rodríguez was killed.

Protection machinery exists and has been used. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging that conflict-driven violence against these individuals constitutes gender persecution, a crime against humanity. The UN Human Rights Committee has registered concern over the same pattern, and a Colombian court has ruled on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty, protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system.
tangentialFactors:
The violence recorded in Antioquia sits inside a national pattern that spans both urban and conflict-affected settings. Targeted killings of trans people continue in ordinary urban areas, as the Bello case shows, while departments under armed-group control see pre-announced kill lists and flyer campaigns that name trans people explicitly. Both conditions apply to a visitor moving between cities and rural areas.

National kill tallies for 2023 and early 2024 are drawn from national reporting rather than from Antioquia-specific records, and they describe the country as a whole. The southern-department 'social cleansing' flyers are documented for Caquetá, not Antioquia; they indicate the environment a trans traveller crosses when moving between departments rather than a condition specific to Medellín or Bello.

The official response to the Bello killing was substantial: a presidential order for investigation, vigils and solidarity events in several cities, and international media coverage. The same response exposed institutional conduct, since the Attorney General's Office's own homicide counts continue to rise and the UN Independent Expert judged the country's legal reforms disconnected from lived experience.

Legal gender recognition, marriage equality and non-binary identification markers are national entitlements, so a trans visitor holding correctly issued documents enters under the same rules as a Colombian resident. What varies regionally is exposure to armed-group activity and to the willingness of local institutions to apply those rules.
localsOnly:
Residents change the sex marker on cédula and other government identification by signing a document before a notary, a route open since June 2015 without judicial authorisation, medical examination or psychiatric assessment. Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993 grounds recognition in self-declaration, and national documents have carried trans and non-binary markers since November 2025.

In the Bello case, the municipal authorities were criticised for using Sara Millerey's pre-transition name in official communication. The same case records a clinic declining to treat her as an emergency on the stated ground that she had not been shot, and her death from cardiac arrest the following afternoon.

Colombians living in departments with armed-group presence face announced campaigns of 'social cleansing' and named kill lists. Trans women in Caquetá reported few livelihood options beyond sex work, and two named trans residents were forced to relocate or lost close contacts to killing and death threats.

Protection is available through two channels that have produced outcomes: ordinary courts, which have ruled on the treatment of trans women deprived of liberty, and the Special Jurisdiction for Peace, which in July 2023 charged 15 former rebels with gender persecution as a crime against humanity. A comprehensive trans law remained before the legislature in 2025, so existing entitlements rest on constitutional and administrative measures rather than on a single statute.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not source how the Bello case is being charged. Whether prosecutors have proceeded as femicide, an aggravated hate crime or ordinary homicide is unresolved here, as is whether the clinic's refusal of treatment was investigated.

Reporting gives the attack as 4 April 2025 and the video as circulating from 5 April; the exact sequence of the assault and the filming is not independently sourced in the inventory.

The 2023 and early 2024 national kill tallies, and the Caquetá flyer campaign, come from national and international reporting with no Antioquia-specific corroboration in this inventory. Antioquia departmental figures for anti-trans killings are not sourced and are not stated.

No source in the inventory documents Antioquia police protocol for handling anti-trans complaints, the practical processing time for a notary-based marker change in Medellín, or hate-crime sentencing outcomes in the department. These remain not sourced rather than confirmed absent.
